title: Sleep softly
hookLine: an unnamed nun is told: sleep softly in the robe you made, your passion stilled like herbs dried in a pot (Therigatha 1.1)

cards: A robe, sewn by the woman who will wear it. A pot on a shelf where herbs have dried out. And a voice saying: sleep softly.
That's nearly the whole of the first poem in the Therigatha. It's only a few lines long, and the nun it speaks to has no name. The heading calls her a certain elder nun, and that's all.
The book of the nuns' own words opens not with a queen or a well-known teacher, but with a woman nobody wrote down by name.

teach.b: First, the nun with no name. Some readers find a quiet welcome in that: the first words of the collection go to someone whose name wasn't kept. She could be anyone who sat in a robe and practiced.
She is told to sleep softly, wrapped in the robe she made herself. Her rest isn't borrowed; she's resting inside her own work. Third, the herbs.

teach.h: LIKE HERBS DRIED IN A POT.
teach.b: The reason she can sleep, the voice says, is that her passion is stilled, like herbs dried in a pot. Green leaves are full of sap. Leave them in a pot and the moisture goes out of them.
They don't fight. They just dry. The craving that used to pull at her has lost its sap the same way, with nothing left in it to sprout.
Fourth, what the poem asks of her. Not to strive harder, not to teach anyone, not to prove anything. It says sleep.
Freedom, in this first poem, is rest after long work.

In Pali the phrase is sukham supahi, sleep at ease, and sukha is the ordinary word for ease and happiness, the word that stands across from dukkha, suffering. So the book of the nuns begins with permission.

how: Readers of the Therigatha meet this short poem first, and teachers in some Buddhist communities use it to speak about rest and contentment as part of the path, not a break from it.

o: rest at ease, with craving stilled
a rule to sleep less and practice more
a bedtime prayer nuns say each night

games.q: the first poem: tap the pairs.

s: the Therigatha opens with a poem by a well-known queen
it opens with a nun whose name wasn't kept: a certain elder nun.
in the poem, her passion is compared to herbs dried in a pot
the sap has gone out of the craving, the way it goes out of herbs in a pot.
the poem tells her to keep striving harder
it tells her to sleep softly, wrapped in the robe she made.

games.q: you're the nun in the first poem. your passion is stilled. a voice beside you says one thing. what does it say?
o: now go and teach the others.
sleep softly, in the robe you made.
games.why: the first poem of the nuns' book is permission to rest: sleep softly, wrapped in your own work.

practice: Find one thing nearby that your own hands made or shaped: a meal, a made bed, a folded sweater, a page you wrote, or one from memory if nothing is within reach.
Let your attention rest on it the way she rested in her robe, with nothing to improve and nothing to add.

wordCard.voice: Sleep softly. The first poem of the Therigatha: a nun with no name, told to rest in the robe she made, her passion stilled like herbs dried in a pot. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sukhaṃ supāhi: sleep at ease, sleep softly. The opening words of the poem.

carryVoice: Your line: herbs dried in a pot. A woman told she can lie down, wrapped in what she made, with nothing tugging at her. Day seven hundred eighty-two.
